q: What are the CIP configurations of the three stereocenters of open-chain D-fructose (shown)?
h: Rank OH first and H last at each center, then decide which carbon branch (up or down) wins. H is on a horizontal bond, toward you.
w: At C3 the C2 branch (C=O: O,O,C) beats C4 (O,C,H). At C4, C3 (O,C,H) ties C5 (O,C,H) at the first atoms, but further out C3 leads to the ketone carbon while C5 leads to CH2OH, so C3 wins. At C5, C4 (O,C,H) beats CH2OH (O,H,H). So the upward carbon is always priority 2. With H toward the viewer, a right-side OH gives R and a left-side OH gives S: left, right, right = (3S,4R,5R) (confirmed with CIP software).
x: This inverts every center: it is L-fructose. It comes from forgetting that the horizontal H points toward you.
C3 has its –OH on the left, which gives S, not R.
C4 has its –OH on the right; with the C3 branch outranking C5 that center is R.

q: β-D-Mannopyranose is shown. In its more stable chair (the <sup>4</sup>C<sub>1</sub> chair, with CH<sub>2</sub>OH equatorial), which ring substituent is axial?
c: None; all five substituents are equatorial
h: Start from β-D-glucopyranose, where every substituent is equatorial in this chair. How does mannose differ from glucose?
w: In the 4C1 chair β-D-glucopyranose has all substituents equatorial. D-Mannose is the C2 epimer of glucose, so inverting C2 moves only that –OH, from equatorial to axial. β-D-Mannopyranose therefore has the C2 –OH axial and everything else equatorial.
x: The C1 –OH is axial in α anomers. In β-mannose it is cis to CH<sub>2</sub>OH and equatorial, as in β-glucose.
The C4 –OH of mannose has the same configuration as in glucose (equatorial). An axial C4 –OH is the mark of galactose.
That is true only for β-D-glucopyranose. Mannose differs from glucose at C2, so one group must be axial.

q: Heating D-glucose in methanol with a little HCl converts only the C1 –OH into –OCH<sub>3</sub> (giving a mixture of methyl α- and β-glucosides). Why does only the anomeric –OH react?
c: Loss of water from C1 gives an oxocarbenium ion stabilized by the ring oxygen
The C1 –OH is the most acidic, so methoxide attacks C1 by S<sub>N</sub>2 and displaces it
The other –OH groups are protected by hydrogen bonds to the methanol solvent
C1 is the only primary carbon in the ring, so it reacts fastest with methanol
h: Under acid, which carbon can lose –OH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> to give the most stabilized cation?
w: Acid protonates the anomeric –OH, and water leaves to give a cyclic oxocarbenium ion, in which the ring O lone pair forms a C=O+ π bond. No other ring carbon has an adjacent oxygen that can stabilize a cation, so only C1 ionizes (an SN1-like acetal formation). Methanol adds to either face of the planar ion, which is why both anomers form.
x: The conditions are acidic: there is no methoxide, and an S<sub>N</sub>2 at C1 would give only one anomer, not a mixture.
Hydrogen bonding to solvent does not protect an alcohol. The other OH groups are simply not ionized because their cations would not be stabilized.
C1 is a secondary carbon bonded to two oxygens. The only primary carbon is C6 (CH<sub>2</sub>OH), which does not react under these conditions.

q: A disaccharide made of two D-glucopyranose units is treated with excess CH3I and Ag2O, then hydrolyzed with aqueous acid. The products are 2,3,4,6-tetra-O-methyl-D-glucose and 2,3,4-tri-O-methyl-D-glucose. What is the glycosidic linkage?
h: Methylation caps every free –OH. Acid hydrolysis then cleaves only acetal bonds (the glycosidic bond and any methyl glycosides). Which –OH groups were not free before methylation?
w: After hydrolysis an unmethylated –OH marks an oxygen that was tied up in a ring or a glycosidic bond. The tetramethyl unit has free C1 and C5 only: it is the nonreducing end, joined through its C1 and closed through C5. The trimethyl unit has free C1 and C5 (ring and anomeric carbon) plus a free C6 –OH, so its C6 oxygen carried the glycosidic bond. The linkage is 1→6 (as in isomaltose or gentiobiose).
x: A 1→4 link would leave the second unit's C4 –OH unmethylated, giving 2,3,6-tri-O-methylglucose, not 2,3,4-.
A 1→1 link (as in trehalose) uses both anomeric carbons, so both units would come out as 2,3,4,6-tetramethyl glucose.
A 1→2 link would leave C2 free, giving 3,4,6-tri-O-methylglucose.

q: The disaccharide shown (lactose) is treated with Br<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O and then hydrolyzed with aqueous acid. What are the products?
h: Bromine water oxidizes only a free aldehyde, which comes from a hemiacetal. Which ring still has one?
w: The galactose unit is joined through its anomeric carbon (an acetal), so it cannot open. The glucose unit (right) has a free hemiacetal at C1, which opens to an aldehyde and is oxidized by Br2/H2O to a carboxylic acid (a lactobionic acid). Acid hydrolysis of the glycosidic bond then releases D-galactose and D-gluconic acid.
x: The galactose C1 is locked in the β(1→4) glycosidic acetal, so it is the unit that cannot be oxidized.
Only one anomeric carbon is free. The galactose C1 is protected as an acetal during the oxidation step.
Lactose is a reducing sugar: its glucose hemiacetal is oxidized before hydrolysis, so glucose comes out as gluconic acid.

q: Alanine has pKa values of 2.34 (α-COOH) and 9.70 (α-NH3+). What is its isoelectric point?
h: For an amino acid with no ionizable side chain, the neutral zwitterion is the major form between the two pKa values.
w: The pI is the pH where the average charge is zero. The zwitterion exists between the two pKa values, and the pI is their average: (2.34 + 9.70)/2 = 6.02.
x: 3.68 is half the difference of the pKa values, not their average.
pH 7.00 is neutral water. An amino acid's pI depends on its own pKa values.
12.04 is the sum of the two pKa values; it still has to be divided by 2.

q: What is the isoelectric point of glutamic acid?
h: Write the charge of each form as the pH rises past each pKa. The pI is the average of the two pKa values on either side of the neutral form.
w: Charges: +1 (below 2.19) → 0 (2.19–4.25) → −1 (4.25–9.67) → −2. The neutral form is flanked by pKa 2.19 and 4.25, so pI = (2.19 + 4.25)/2 = 3.22. An acidic side chain pulls the pI well below 6.
x: 6.96 averages the two pKa values around the −1 form, not the neutral form.
Averaging all three pKa values has no physical meaning; only the two that border the zwitterion count.
5.93 averages the α-COOH and α-NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> values and ignores the side chain, which ionizes before the amino group.

q: What is the isoelectric point of histidine?
h: Is the imidazolium side chain positive or neutral when it holds its proton? Track the net charge from the fully protonated form.
w: Fully protonated histidine is +2 (NH3+ and imidazolium, COOH neutral). Charges: +2 → +1 after 1.82 (COO−) → 0 after 6.00 (neutral imidazole) → −1 after 9.17 (NH2). The neutral form lies between 6.00 and 9.17, so pI = (6.00 + 9.17)/2 = 7.59.
x: 3.91 treats the side chain like a carboxylic acid that becomes negative. Imidazolium goes from +1 to 0 when it loses its proton.
5.50 ignores the side chain. Histidine has an extra positive charge at low pH, which pushes the pI up.
Averaging all three pKa values is not how a pI is found.

q: Aspartic acid has pKa values of 1.88 (α-COOH), 3.65 (side-chain COOH) and 9.60 (α-NH3+). Which form is the major species at pH 3.0?
h: Compare pH with each pKa: a group is mostly deprotonated when pH > pKa and mostly protonated when pH < pKa.
w: At pH 3.0: the α-COOH (1.88) is above its pKa, so it is mostly COO−; the side-chain COOH (3.65) is below its pKa, so it is mostly COOH; the amine (9.60) is NH3+. The major species is the zwitterion with a neutral side-chain COOH.
x: Fully protonated (+1) aspartic acid is the major form only below pH 1.88.
The α-COOH (pKa 1.88) is more acidic than the side-chain COOH (3.65), because the nearby NH3+ withdraws electron density. It loses its proton first.
The −1 form, with both carboxylates, is major between pH 3.65 and 9.60.

q: What is the approximate net charge of the tripeptide Gly-His-Asp at pH 7.0?
h: Only the two termini and the side chains ionize; the amide N–H groups do not. Compare pH 7.0 with each pKa.
w: At pH 7.0: C-terminal COO− (−1); Asp side-chain COO− (−1); His is 1 unit above its pKa, so only about 9% is protonated (≈ 0); the N-terminal NH3+ is 1 unit below its pKa, so about 91% is protonated (≈ +1). Net ≈ −1.
x: This counts His as +1. At pH 7.0, one unit above its pKa, the imidazole is mostly neutral.
This counts His as +1 and misses the Asp side-chain carboxylate.
This forgets the N-terminal NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, which is still mostly protonated at pH 7.0.

q: L-Serine is (S) but L-cysteine is (R), although the two have the same spatial arrangement at the α carbon. What is the reason?
c: Sulfur outranks oxygen, so CH<sub>2</sub>SH outranks CO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>; in serine CH<sub>2</sub>OH ranks below it
L-Cysteine has its NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> on the opposite side of the Fischer projection from L-serine
The SH group is the lowest-priority group in cysteine, so the H moves to priority 3
D and L are defined by the CIP rules, so the two labels must agree for every amino acid
h: Rank the four groups at each α carbon. At the first point of difference, compare (O,O,O) for the carboxylate with (S,H,H) or (O,H,H) for the side chain.
w: Both have NH3+ = 1 and H = 4. In serine, CO2− (O,O,O) beats CH2OH (O,H,H). In cysteine, CH2SH has (S,H,H), and S (Z = 16) beats O (Z = 8) at the first point of difference, so the side chain outranks the carboxylate. Priorities 2 and 3 swap, so the same arrangement is labeled R.
x: Both are L amino acids: in the Fischer projection (COOH on top) the NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> is on the left for both. The spatial arrangement is the same.
H is always lowest priority. The SH is not even on the stereocenter; it is on the β carbon.
D/L describes the Fischer arrangement relative to glyceraldehyde; R/S comes from CIP priorities. The two systems are independent, which is exactly why they can disagree.

q: Which amino acid is shown in the Fischer projection?
h: With COOH on top and the side chain on the bottom, which side does the amino group of an L amino acid occupy?
w: With COOH on top, L amino acids have NH2 on the left; here it is on the right, so this is a D amino acid. CIP: NH2 > COOH > CH3 > H. NH2 (right) → COOH (top) → CH3 (bottom) runs counterclockwise, and H is on a horizontal bond toward the viewer, so the label reverses to R: D-alanine, (R).
x: L-Alanine has NH<sub>2</sub> on the left. This drawing is its mirror image.
The counterclockwise path must be reversed because the H points toward the viewer, which gives R.
L and R do not go together for alanine; natural L-alanine is S.

q: Natural L-threonine is (2S,3R)-2-amino-3-hydroxybutanoic acid. Which Fischer projection represents it?
h: Assign each center separately. At C3 rank OH > C2 (N,C,H) > CH<sub>3</sub> > H.
w: C2: an L amino acid has NH2 on the left (S). C3: OH > C2 > CH3; with OH on the right, OH → C2 (up) → CH3 (down) runs counterclockwise, reversed to R because H points toward the viewer. NH2 left and OH right is IV, (2S,3R) (confirmed with CIP software).
x: I is (2S,3S): L-allothreonine, the C3 epimer.
II is (2R,3S): D-threonine, the enantiomer of L-threonine.
III is (2R,3R): D-allothreonine.

q: Which carbonyl compound gives valine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)–COOH, in a Strecker synthesis (1. NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, KCN 2. H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, heat)?
h: The carbonyl carbon becomes the α carbon (it gains NH<sub>2</sub> and CN, and the CN becomes COOH). Work backward from the side chain.
w: In the Strecker synthesis the aldehyde forms an imine with NH3, cyanide adds to give an α-aminonitrile, and hydrolysis converts CN to COOH. The aldehyde carbon becomes the α carbon, and everything attached to it becomes the side chain. Valine's side chain is isopropyl, so the aldehyde is 2-methylpropanal. The product is racemic, because cyanide adds equally to both faces of the planar imine.
x: 3-Methylbutanal has one more CH<sub>2</sub>, so it gives leucine (isobutyl side chain).
Propanal gives 2-aminobutanoic acid, with an ethyl side chain.
Acetone is a ketone. It gives 2-amino-2-methylpropanoic acid, with two methyls on the α carbon.

q: In the chair, the α anomer of D-glucopyranose has its C1 –OH axial. Based on A-values alone it should be only a few percent of the equilibrium mixture, but it is about 36%. What extra stabilization does an axial electronegative group at C1 receive?
c: Donation of a ring-oxygen lone pair into the σ* orbital of the axial C1–O bond
Hydrogen bonding of the axial C1 –OH to the axial hydrogens on C3 and C5
Conjugation of the C1 –OH with the C2–C3 bond, which is possible only when it is axial
A lower steric demand for –OH than for H, so –OH prefers the axial position
h: This is the anomeric effect. Which orbitals are antiperiplanar when the C1–O bond is axial?
w: When the C1–O bond is axial, it is antiperiplanar to a lone pair on the ring oxygen. That filled n orbital overlaps with the empty σ*(C1–O) orbital (hyperconjugation), which stabilizes the axial anomer. Dipole repulsion between the ring C–O bonds is also smaller. This anomeric effect offsets part of the steric penalty, so α-glucose is 36% instead of a few percent.
x: Axial hydrogens on C3 and C5 are C–H bonds and are not hydrogen-bond acceptors. The axial –OH actually suffers 1,3-diaxial steric strain from them.
C2–C3 is a σ bond with no π system, so there is nothing to conjugate with.
–OH is larger than H (A-value about 0.9 kcal/mol in cyclohexane), so steric effects favor the equatorial position, not the axial one.
